explainedBy: A commercial strategist pores over fictional consumer avatars while disregarding real context.

storyboard.claim: Marketers construct fictional consumer personas while ignoring immediate reality.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Marketer in a sleek agency boardroom holds demographic profile notes with an overconfident smirk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Connects the demographic obsession from beat 43 to the fictional avatars marketers create.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the corporate boardroom setting where demographic profiles are drafted far from real buying moments.

explainedBy: The everyday consumer navigates immediate environmental pressure while marketers focus solely on demographics.

storyboard.claim: Immediate situational feelings and physical context dictate behavior over static identities.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper walks briskly down a crowded sidewalk, looking overwhelmed by immediate surroundings.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the marketer's boardroom abstraction in beat 44 with the consumer's immediate reality.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the physical and emotional stress of the actual buyer in the split second of choice.

explainedBy: The host introduces Darley and Batson's landmark 1973 Princeton experiment on situational behavior.

storyboard.claim: The 1973 Princeton Good Samaritan study rigorously tested whether character predicts behavior.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Marketer speaks beside an experimental notes icon referencing the famous 1973 Princeton study.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the central psychological study demonstrating situational dominance over character.
storyboard.addedInformation: Anchors the discussion in historic academic research on human decision-making.

explainedBy: The experiment selected trainee priests to test whether proclaimed moral character dictates real-world action.

storyboard.claim: The experiment tested trainee priests whose entire vocation was defined by moral virtue.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper holds a theological scripture book with a serious, contemplative expression in a quiet room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Establishes the subject pool: trainee priests chosen specifically for their explicit moral commitment.
storyboard.addedInformation: Emphasizes the religious study context to set up the baseline expectation of high moral integrity.

explainedBy: The subjects are dedicated seminary students whose stated purpose is altruism and moral devotion.

storyboard.claim: The seminary students were dedicated by explicit life goals to helping others.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper continues holding the sacred book in the study room, looking earnest.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the character profile of beat 47, reinforcing their theoretical altruism.
storyboard.addedInformation: Highlights the explicit vocational oath of the participants before situational pressure is applied.

explainedBy: A seminary student walks across campus carrying his speech notes to record a presentation.

storyboard.claim: Subjects were instructed to walk across campus to record an assigned presentation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper walks along a campus pathway icon holding lecture notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves the student from the preparation room onto the outdoor physical journey.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets the physical stage where the unexpected situational hurdle will appear.

explainedBy: The presentation topic assigned to the student is the parable of the Good Samaritan, establishing the experimental irony.

storyboard.claim: Some students were assigned to lecture on the Good Samaritan parable itself.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper continues along the campus street holding the presentation notes on the Good Samaritan.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reveals the speech topic, heightening the dramatic irony of their upcoming moral test.
storyboard.addedInformation: Underlines that the moral principle was literally top-of-mind for the subjects.

explainedBy: The researchers introduce time pressure as the lone experimental variable testing moral behavior.

storyboard.claim: Researchers introduced a single manipulated variable: time pressure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Marketer points toward a prominent clock icon, representing the experimental manipulation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the single independent variable that will test the seminary students' convictions.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames time pressure as the psychological trap designed by Darley and Batson.

explainedBy: A sorter diagram displays the low hurry and medium hurry experimental conditions.

storyboard.claim: Researchers divided the students into varying hurry conditions to test behavioral variance.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sorter diagram displays buckets for LOW HURRY and MEDIUM HURRY conditions.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Breaks down the time pressure variable into the first two experimental groups.
storyboard.addedInformation: Structures the experimental methodology so the viewer sees the graded time conditions.

explainedBy: The sorter diagram completes the three-tier experimental hurry structure with the high hurry condition.

storyboard.claim: A third group was subjected to severe hurry by being told they were already late.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The sorter diagram expands to include the HIGH HURRY bucket alongside the previous two.
storyboard.onScreenText: LOW HURRY | MEDIUM HURRY | HIGH HURRY
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the three experimental cohorts with the high hurry group.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the full spectrum of time pressure tested in the Princeton study.

explainedBy: The researchers placed an actor slumped in an alleyway directly along the students' route.

storyboard.claim: Researchers staged an apparently injured actor slumped in an alleyway along the path.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper, acting as the test victim, slumps in distress against a wall in an alleyway.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from the experimental conditions to the actual physical staging of the obstacle.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the physical arrangement of the staged emergency facing the subjects.

explainedBy: A passing theology student encounters the slumped actor groaning in distress on the alleyway pavement.

storyboard.claim: The slumped actor audibly groaned and coughed, creating an unmistakable distress signal.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper walks down the alley past The Marketer, who slumps against the wall in visible pain.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings the passing student into direct physical encounter with the slumped actor from beat 54.
storyboard.addedInformation: Stages the critical moment of encounter where moral duty confronts situational pressure.

callout.text: STOP TO HELP A DYING MAN

explainedBy: The expected moral response is for the pious student to stop and reach out to assist the suffering man.

storyboard.claim: Common sense predicts a pious theology student would immediately stop to help.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper pauses and reaches an outstretched hand toward the slumped figure.
storyboard.onScreenText: STOP TO HELP A DYING MAN
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Depicts the intuitive moral hypothesis before revealing the experimental finding.
storyboard.addedInformation: Dramatizes the expected altruistic response dictated by religious training.

explainedBy: The theology student walks straight past the suffering man, showing moral identity failed to produce aid.

storyboard.claim: Religious vocation and moral character failed to predict helping behavior.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper walks past the slumped figure with a detached expression, ignoring his groans.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Subverts the expected helping behavior from beat 56 as the student walks away.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the stark failure of character traits when confronted with situational constraints.

explainedBy: A cause-and-effect flow connects injected time pressure directly to the decision to stop and help.

storyboard.claim: Time pressure was the only statistically significant predictor of helping behavior.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow diagram maps TIME PRESSURE directly to STOP TO HELP.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Identifies the actual scientific driver behind whether students aided the victim.
storyboard.addedInformation: Eliminates vague assumptions by isolating the exact causal mechanism proven by the data.

explainedBy: Over six in ten theology students stopped to assist when under minimal time pressure.

storyboard.claim: In the low hurry condition, 63% of the seminary students stopped to offer help.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper stands calmly on the sidewalk pointing toward the 63% statistic.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Presents the statistical baseline showing high helping rates when hurry was absent.
storyboard.addedInformation: Proves that students were willing to help when environmental context permitted it.

explainedBy: Under intense time pressure, rushed students literally stepped over the collapsed man to meet their deadline.

storyboard.claim: In the high hurry condition, only 10% stopped, with some stepping over the victim.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper rushes forward with urgent strides past The Marketer, who lies collapsed on the ground.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the 63% low-hurry rate with the dramatic 10% helping rate under time stress.
storyboard.addedInformation: Captures the startling detail of theology students physically stepping over an injured body.

explainedBy: The host reflects on how external situational context completely overrides internal personality.

storyboard.claim: Immediate situational context entirely governed moral choice rather than personality.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Marketer reflects with a troubled expression in an office, processing the unsettling findings.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Summarizes the philosophical and psychological takeaway from the Princeton study.
storyboard.addedInformation: Underscores the blow to human ego when realizing situation overpowers moral self-image.

explainedBy: Richard Shotton applies the situational findings to advertising through Lumen Research's eye-tracking data.

storyboard.claim: Lumen Research eye-tracking data demonstrates identical situational effects in digital advertising.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Marketer reviews eye-tracking behavioral data on an open laptop in an agency office.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from the Princeton psychological experiment to modern digital consumer behavior.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces eye-tracking empirical data to demonstrate situational blindness in digital ads.

explainedBy: A hurried consumer scrolls rapidly on their smartphone with tunnel vision, barely noticing screen ads.

storyboard.claim: Digital ads viewed for less than a second fail to achieve meaningful brand recall.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper sits in a busy cafe rapidly flicking through a smartphone screen with tunnel vision.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Details the specific finding of the Lumen eye-tracking study on brief ad exposures.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows how mobile haste creates cognitive tunnel vision that blinds consumers to advertising.

explainedBy: A hurried consumer locks eyes on their path and screen, ignoring all surrounding brand advertising.

storyboard.claim: A rushing consumer's cognitive map narrows exclusively to immediate operational goals.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper walks briskly down the street with gaze fixed on a smartphone and an immediate target icon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the psychological mechanism causing the sub-second ad blindness from beat 63.
storyboard.addedInformation: Illustrates goal-directed attention filtering out all peripheral commercial stimuli.

explainedBy: A marketer slumped over pitch notes realizes that even superior ads fail against hostile temporal context.

storyboard.claim: Even compelling creative executions fail when delivered in an unreceptive temporal context.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Marketer slumps over advertising campaign notes in an empty conference room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the core marketing implication: message quality cannot overcome hostile timing.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts creative craft with the overwhelming veto power of consumer situational context.

explainedBy: The skeptic co-host challenges the theory, arguing income and demographic data must establish buying choices.

storyboard.claim: A skeptical counterargument asks whether income and demographics still set core buying choices.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper holds a wallet while sporting a skeptical smirk in a retail showroom.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the devil's advocate pushback defending traditional demographic targeting.
storyboard.addedInformation: Articulates the intuitive consumer assumption that income dictates buying behavior.

explainedBy: The skeptic asserts that stable personal preferences outweigh transient rush in purchasing decisions.

storyboard.claim: Personal tastes and political beliefs intuitively seem more influential than momentary hurry.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper continues speaking while holding their wallet in the retail showroom.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Expands the devil's advocate objection to include enduring taste and personal politics.
storyboard.addedInformation: Voices the belief that enduring identity traits govern major purchase choices.

explainedBy: The speaker poses a vivid extreme: a wealthy traveler buys a luxury watch regardless of flight stress.

storyboard.claim: A stressed millionaire at an airport still buys a luxury watch rather than a cheap alternative.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper smiles wryly while holding a gold coin before luxury retail displays.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Provides a concrete luxury product comparison testing the limits of situational context.
storyboard.addedInformation: Uses the Rolex versus cheap watch scenario to illustrate demographic boundary conditions.

explainedBy: The strategist concedes that income establishes the non-negotiable ceiling of what a consumer can buy.

storyboard.claim: Income creates a hard boundary of affordability that heuristics cannot bypass.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Marketer points to an economic diagram illustrating income ceilings.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concedes the financial constraint argument before clarifying where context actually operates.
storyboard.addedInformation: Validates the reality that consumer heuristics cannot manufacture unpossessed funds.

explainedBy: Marketers mistakenly rely on fixed personal traits rather than recognizing context as the ultimate selector.

storyboard.claim: Within affordable options, marketers place unwarranted faith in fixed personality traits.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper looks worried while holding a wallet, with 'FAITH IN STABLE TRAITS' struck through.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Rebuts the demographic assumption by rejecting excessive reliance on fixed character traits.
storyboard.addedInformation: Uses a strike-through to formally reject the theory that traits govern in-moment choices.

explainedBy: While demographics define options, immediate context acts as the decisive trigger for purchase.

storyboard.claim: Demographics provide the realm of possibility, but immediate context pulls the trigger.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Marketer points forward with conviction beside an aiming target icon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the core theoretical synthesis resolving demographics versus context.
storyboard.addedInformation: Encapsulates the central thesis: possibility is demographic, but action is contextual.

explainedBy: Targeting consumers purely by income or stated preferences fails without considering situational context.

storyboard.claim: Targeting based solely on income or preferences is functionally useless without context.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Marketer holds demographic target notes with a frustrated expression as the strategy is struck out.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Translates the trigger principle into an explicit indictment of income-only media targeting.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strikes through income-only targeting to warn brands against wasteful demographic spending.

explainedBy: A hurried traveler frantically stares at their phone, lacking the cognitive capacity to notice ads.

storyboard.claim: Persuasion requires catching consumers when they have available cognitive bandwidth.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper rushes across an airport concourse staring anxiously at flight updates on a smartphone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the contextual trigger rule to mental bandwidth during stressful travel moments.
storyboard.addedInformation: Depicts consumer cognitive overload where high-income targets ignore luxury brand messages.

explainedBy: Situational context consistently outweighs demographic identity in determining real-world attention and choices.

storyboard.claim: Immediate environmental context consistently overrules static demographic categories.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Marketer speaks authoritatively beside a tipped balance scale icon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Establishes the foundational conclusion linking the Good Samaritan study to commerce.
storyboard.addedInformation: Uses the balance scale to represent context definitively outweighing demographics.

explainedBy: Consumers rely on subconscious cognitive shortcuts rather than calculating purchase decisions rationally.

storyboard.claim: Purchasing decisions are predictable heuristic shortcuts rather than rational calculations.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper pauses thoughtfully before retail aisles beside an illuminating lightbulb icon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines the core psychological mechanism that replaces rational demographic models.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the central concept of the Choice Factory: predictable heuristic shortcuts.

explainedBy: The commercial strategist manipulates choice architecture through physical friction and perceptual framing.

storyboard.claim: Heuristic shortcuts are triggered by immediate context, friction, and psychological framing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Marketer gestures toward marketing strategy concepts on a boardroom whiteboard with a confident smirk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the tactical levers that marketers use to steer heuristic shortcuts.
storyboard.addedInformation: Connects behavioral theory to concrete commercial architecture: friction and framing.

explainedBy: The hosts shift from internal mental rush to external social influence and the power of crowds.

storyboard.claim: The presence of other people constitutes the most powerful external context of all.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A wide crowd shot shows The Shopper walking among multiple pedestrians on a bustling street.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pivots from internal psychological pressure (hurry) to external social environments.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces social dynamics as the supreme environmental force driving choices.

explainedBy: The hosts formally introduce social proof as the next major behavioral bias in the Choice Factory.

storyboard.claim: Social proof emerges as the dominant behavioral shortcut governing social beings.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper pauses on the pavement, looking around with a spark of recognition.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the specific behavioral bias arising from the presence of other people.
storyboard.addedInformation: Transitions from general social context to the formal bias of social proof.

callout.text: PULL UP TO A RED LIGHT

explainedBy: A commuter stops at a traffic signal and glances over toward pedestrians on the sidewalk.

storyboard.claim: A driver pauses at a red light during a routine commute and notices pedestrians.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper sits patiently at a street intersection, glancing toward the adjacent sidewalk.
storyboard.onScreenText: PULL UP TO A RED LIGHT
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens a narrative thought experiment illustrating social proof in action.
storyboard.addedInformation: Establishes a familiar, routine everyday scenario to stage the social reflex.

explainedBy: A group of pedestrians cranes their necks and stares fixatedly toward something high above.

storyboard.claim: A group of pedestrians on the sidewalk stands craning their necks, staring into the sky.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper looks upward with raised chin and a pointed finger toward the sky.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Depicts the unusual pedestrian behavior that catches the driver's attention.
storyboard.addedInformation: Illustrates the visual cue of collective upward gaze triggering curiosity.

explainedBy: The crowd's collective gaze is locked on the high branches of a tall oak tree.

storyboard.claim: The pedestrians focus their collective gaze on the high branches of an oak tree.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Shopper points toward a large tree icon standing against the street backdrop.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reveals the focal point of the crowd's gaze, setting the trap for beat 82.
storyboard.addedInformation: Provides the tangible physical landmark that draws the driver's involuntary gaze.
